fetched_contents.text: Sexual Response Cycle: Order, Phases & What To Know What is the sexual response cycle? The sexual response cycle is the sequence of physical and emotional changes that occur as a person becomes sexually aroused and participates in sexually stimulating activities, including intercourse and masturbation. Knowing how your body responds during each phase of the cycle can enhance your relationship and help you pinpoint causes of sexual dysfunction. Cleveland Clinic is a non-profit academic medical center. Advertising on our site helps support our mission. We do not endorse non-Cleveland Clinic products or services. Policy What are the four phases of the human sexual response? The sexual response cycle has four phases: 1. Desire (libido or excitement) 2. Arousal (sometimes called plateau) 3. Orgasm 4. Resolution Males and females can experience these phases, although the timing may be different. For example, it’s highly unlikely that both partners will reach orgasm at the exact same time. In addition, the intensity of the response and the time spent in each phase varies from person to person. Some people may skip a phase entirely. Some of these stages may be absent during certain sexual encounters, or out of sequence in others. A desire for intimacy may be a motivation for sexual activity in some individuals but could be less for others. Understanding these differences may help partners better understand one another’s bodies. It can help you understand your partner’s responses and enhance your overall sexual experience. What is the shortest sexual response cycle? Orgasm is the shortest stage of the sexual response cycle. What is the order of the stages of sexual response? There are four stages of human sexual response: desire, arousal, orgasm and resolution. Keep in mind, that the order and timing of the stages can vary. Phase 1: Desire General characteristics of this phase, which can last from a few minutes to several hours, may include any of the following: * Muscle tension increases. * Heart rate quickens and breathing gets faster. * Skin may become flushed (blotches may appear on your chest and back). * Nipples become hardened or erect. * Blood flow to your genitals increases, which causes swelling of the clitoris and an erection. * If you have a vagina, you may feel it get “wet” or see your breasts become fuller. * If you have a penis, you may see your testicles swell or your scrotum (sac that holds testicles) tighten, and you may begin secreting a lubricating liquid from the tip of your penis. It’s important to note that everyone’s sexual experience is different. You may not consistently experience any changes when you enter the desire phase. You may experience it during certain sexual encounters only. Sometimes, the desire phase may come after arousal. Phase 2: Arousal The arousal phase lasts until just before orgasm. It takes you to the brink of sexual pleasure and could include: * The changes in the desire phase get even more intense. * The vagina continues to swell from increased blood flow, and the vaginal walls turn a darker color. * The clitoris becomes highly sensitive (may even be painful to touch). * The testicles withdraw up into the scrotum. * Breathing, heart rate and blood pressure continue to increase. * Muscle tension continues to increase. * Muscle spasms may begin in the feet, face and hands. You might experience arousal at the same time as desire or shortly before. Phase 3: Orgasm This phase is the climax of the sexual response cycle. It’s the shortest of the phases and generally lasts only a few seconds. The orgasm phase can include: * Involuntary muscle contractions or twitching. * Blood pressure, heart rate and breathing are at their highest rates. * There’s a sudden, forceful release of sexual tension. * Contraction of vaginal muscles. * Ejaculation (releasing semen from your penis). * A rash or “sex flush” may appear over your entire body. Phase 4: Resolution During this phase, your body slowly returns to its normal level of functioning. Any swollen or erect body parts return to their previous size or position. People may feel a sense of satisfaction and, often, fatigue. Some females can go back to the orgasm phase with further sexual stimulation and may experience additional orgasms. Males typically need recovery time after orgasm, called a refractory period, during which they can’t reach orgasm again. The duration of the refractory period varies and changes with age. What age does arousal start? Like most aspects of the sexual response cycle, the exact age at which a person begins feeling arousal (or desire) varies. Sexual arousal can begin for some people shortly before puberty. Children as young as 10 to 13 may experience sexual attraction or excitement. One study shows that people report experiencing their first orgasm around age 13 to 17. Other studies show it’s normal for children as young as 7 to begin feeling sexual desire. At what age does a person stop ejaculating? Ejaculation doesn’t stop at a certain age. But males may start experiencing erectile dysfunction or other sexual dysfunction in their 40s and 50s. This can lead to ejaculating less frequently. When females enter menopause, many who once ejaculated say they notice changes in ejaculation and orgasm. The sexual response cycle describes the changes that occur during sexual or intimate activities. It provides a pretty good outline, but it’s not a one-size-fits-all model. People go through the four phases at different rates and at varying intensity levels. It’s mostly meant to help people understand their bodies and their partners’ bodies so they can identify sexual dysfunction.

Abstract In men and women sexual arousal culminates in orgasm, with female orgasm solely from sexual intercourse often regarded as a unique feature of human sexuality. However, orgasm from sexual intercourse occurs more reliably in men than in women likely reflecting the different types of physical stimulation men and women require for orgasm. In men, orgasms are under strong selective pressure as orgasms are coupled with ejaculation and thus contribute to male reproductive success. By contrast, women's orgasms in intercourse are highly variable and are under little selective pressure as they are not a reproductive necessity.. The proximal mechanisms producing variability in women's orgasms are little understood. In 1924 Marie Bonaparte proposed that a shorter distance between a woman's clitoris and her urethral meatus (CUMD) increased her likelihood of experiencing orgasm in intercourse. She based this on her published data which were never statistically analyzed. In 1940 Landis and colleagues published similar data suggesting the same relationship, but these data too were never fully analyzed. We analyzed raw data from these two studies and found that both demonstrate a strong inverse relationship between CUMD and orgasm during intercourse. Unresolved is whether this increased likelihood of orgasm with shorter CUMD reflects increased penile-clitoral contact during sexual intercourse or increased penile stimulation of internal aspects of the clitoris. CUMD likely reflects prenatal androgen exposure, with higher androgen levels producing larger distances. Thus these results suggest that women exposed to lower levels of prenatal androgens are more likely to experience orgasm during sexual intercourse. Keywords: orgasm in intercourse, genital anatomy, sex differences, clitoral position, prenatal androgens Introduction Although approximately 90% of women report orgasm from some form of sexual stimulation, most women do not routinely (and some never) experience orgasm solely from sexual intercourse (Lloyd, 2005). By contrast, nearly 100% of men routinely experience orgasm solely from sexual intercourse. This gender disparity in the reliability of reaching orgasm during sexual intercourse has been thought to reflect evolutionary (Lloyd, 2005) or social (Hite, 1976) processes. An anatomical explanation for this disparity has also been proposed such that variation in the distance between a woman's clitoral glans and her vagina predicts the likelihood that she will experience orgasm in intercourse (Narjani, 1924). Specifically it was proposed that if this distance is less than 2.5cm a woman is very likely to have orgasms solely from sexual intercourse. This relationship has not been statistically evaluated, but two historical studies provide data supporting such a relationship (Narjani, 1924; Landis, Landis, and Bowles, 1940). We use an unconventional approach to investigate the proposed relationship between variation in women's genitals and orgasm during intercourse. We first explore the history of this idea in the scientific and popular literature and then present statistical analysis of the two available historical datasets with data relevant to the proposed relationship (Narjani, 1924; Landis, Landis, and Bowles, 1940). While there are challenges to the validity of these data, we find them sufficiently supportive of a relationship between women's genital anatomy and the occurrence of orgasm in intercourse to feel that they can serve as the basis for developing modern well-controlled studies of the relationship between women's genital anatomy and the occurrence of orgasm in intercourse. Orgasm is the culmination of sexual arousal, and the promise of orgasm may provide primary motivation for individuals to engage in sexual intercourse. However, sexual arousal itself is rewarding and likely common to the sexuality of all mammals. Studies of animals have shown that sexual arousal is rewarding even when sexual intercourse doesn't occur (Meisel, Camp and Robinson, 1993). Certainly humans, at least men, sometimes seek out activities, such as strip clubs, where sexual arousal without orgasm is the primary goal and where sexual intercourse is unlikely to occur. In male mammals, sufficient sexual arousal leads to ejaculation and orgasm. Thus it is possible that orgasm occurs in all male mammals. The case in females is less clear. While there is evidence that female sexual arousal is rewarding (Meisel, Camp and Robinson, 1993), it is unclear whether humans, or possibly primates, (Goldfoot, et al., 1980), are unique in being the only animals where heightened female sexual arousal culminates in orgasm. Even in primates female orgasm is not universal, with little evidence of its occurrence outside of humans. Even among women, at least 10% report never having experienced orgasm. To further complicate matters, there remains a lack of complete agreement on what constitutes female orgasm (Meston, et al., 2004; Komisaruk, Beyer-Flores, and Whipple 2006). Although sexual arousal precedes orgasm in women, the specific sexual stimulation that triggers orgasm varies greatly among women. Women reach orgasm from direct clitoral stimulation, indirect clitoral stimulation, vaginal stimulation or stimulation of internal areas surrounding the vagina. Some women experience orgasm solely from sexual intercourse, whereas other women require concurrent stimulation of the external parts of the clitoris in order to reach orgasm during sexual intercourse, and some women never experience orgasm in intercourse under any conditions. fetched_contents.text: Human sexual response cycle Four-stage model of physiological responses to sexual stimulation The human sexual response cycle is a four-stage model of physiological responses to sexual stimulation,[1] which, in order of their occurrence, are the excitement, plateau, orgasmic, and resolution phases.[2][3] This physiological response model was first formulated by William H. Masters and Virginia E. Johnson, in their 1966 book Human Sexual Response.[1][4] Since that time, other models regarding human sexual response have been formulated by several scholars who have criticized certain inaccuracies in the human sexual response cycle model. Excitement phase The excitement phase (also known as the arousal phase or initial excitement phase) is the first stage of the human sexual response cycle, which occurs as a result of physical or mental erotic stimuli, such as kissing, making out, fantasizing or viewing erotic images, that leads to sexual arousal. During this stage, the body prepares for sexual intercourse, initially leading to the plateau phase.[1] There is wide socio-cultural variation regarding preferences for the length of foreplay and the stimulation methods used.[5] Physical and emotional interaction and stimulation of the erogenous zones during foreplay usually establishes at least some initial arousal. Excitement in both sexes See also: Flushing (physiology) Among both sexes, the excitement phase results in an increase in heart rate, breathing rate, and a rise in blood pressure.[1] A survey in 2006 found that sexual arousal in about 82% of young females and 52% of young males arises or is enhanced by direct stimulation of nipples, with only 7–8% reporting that it decreased their arousal.[6] Vasocongestion of the skin, commonly referred to as the sex flush, will occur in approximately 50-75% of females and 25% of males. The sex flush tends to occur more often under warmer conditions and may not appear at all under cooler temperatures. During the female sex flush, pinkish spots develop under the breasts, then spread to the breasts, torso, face, hands, soles of the feet, and possibly over the entire body.[1] Vasocongestion is also responsible for the darkening of the clitoris and the walls of the vagina during sexual arousal. During the male sex flush, the coloration of the skin develops less consistently than in the female, but typically starts with the epigastrium (upper abdomen), spreads across the chest, then continues to the neck, face, forehead, back, and sometimes, shoulders and forearms. The sex flush typically disappears soon after orgasm occurs, but this may take up to two hours or so and, sometimes, intense sweating will occur simultaneously. The flush usually diminishes in reverse of the order in which it appeared.[4] An increase in muscle tone (myotonia) of certain muscle groups, occurring voluntarily and involuntarily, begins during this phase among both sexes.[4] Also, the external anal sphincter may contract randomly upon contact (or later during orgasm without contact). Excitement in males In males, the beginning of the excitement phase is observed when the penis becomes partially or fully erect, often after only a few seconds of erotic stimulation.[1] The erection may be partially lost and regained repeatedly during an extended excitement phase. Both testicles become drawn upward toward the perineum, notably in circumcised males where less skin is available to accommodate the erection. Also, the scrotum can tense and thicken during the erection process. Excitement in females In females, the excitement phase can last from several minutes to several hours. The onset of vasocongestion results in swelling of the woman's clitoris, labia minora and vagina. The muscle that surrounds the vaginal opening grows tighter and the uterus elevates and grows in size. The vaginal walls begin to produce a lubricating organic liquid.[1] Meanwhile, the breasts increase slightly in size and nipples become hardened and erect. Plateau phase See also: Edging (sexual practice) The plateau phase is the period of sexual excitement prior to orgasm. The phase is characterised by an increased circulation and heart rate in both sexes, increased sexual pleasure with increased stimulation and further increased muscle tension. Also, respiration continues at an elevated level.[1] Prolonged time in the plateau phase without progression to the orgasmic phase may result in sexual frustration. Plateau in males During this phase, the male urethral sphincter contracts (preventing urine from mixing with semen, and retrograde ejaculation) and muscles at the base of the penis begin a steady rhythmic contraction.[1] Males may start to secrete seminal fluid or pre-ejaculatory fluid and the testicles rise closer to the body.[4] Plateau in females The plateau stage in females is basically a continuation of the same changes evident in the excitement stage. The clitoris becomes extremely sensitive and withdraws slightly, and the Bartholin glands produce further lubrication. The tissues of the outer third of the vagina swell, and the pubococcygeus muscle tightens, reducing the diameter of the opening of the vagina.[1] Masters and Johnson refer to the changes that take place during the plateau stage as the orgasmic platform. Orgasm phase Main article: Orgasm Orgasm is experienced by both males and females, ending the plateau phase of the sexual response cycle. Orgasm is accompanied by quick cycles of muscle contraction in the lower pelvic muscles, which surround both the anus and the primary sexual organs. Orgasms are often associated with other involuntary actions, including vocalizations and muscular spasms in other areas of the body and a generally euphoric sensation. Heart rate is increased even further.[1] Tantric sex practices may seek to diminish the goal of achieving orgasm, which is frequently a common goal of sexual intercourse. ## Sequential anatomy of human sexual response

The human sexual response sequence, as described in the evidence, is framed around four phases: desire/arousal, plateau, orgasm, and resolution, with the Cleveland Clinic and Wikipedia both identifying this as the standard model [N1-R1][N1-R3]. The anatomical evidence emphasizes that the response is not a single isolated event but a coordinated process involving the brain, genital tract, and autonomic nervous system [N2-R2][N2-R5].

### Anatomical structures active in each phase

**Desire/arousal phase**: The evidence shows that both men and women experience early physiological signs of arousal, including increased heart rate, breathing, and blood pressure [N2-F2][N5-F3]. In men, the phase begins with penile erection, cremaster reflex, and pre-ejaculate; in women, it involves clitoral tumescence, genital vasocongestion, increased vaginal lubrication, and breast changes such as hardened nipples and fuller breasts [N2-R2][N2-R4]. The Cleveland Clinic also notes that the clitoris swells and the vagina swells with increased blood flow, while the breasts become fuller in women [N1-F1]. For men, the testicles may swell or the scrotum may tighten, and the penis may begin to secrete lubricating fluid [N1-F1].

**Plateau phase**: This phase intensifies the arousal process. In men, the evidence states that the urethral sphincter contracts and muscles at the base of the penis begin rhythmic contractions, while the testicles rise closer to the body [N5-F3]. In women, the plateau stage continues the excitement phase changes, with the clitoris becoming extremely sensitive, the Bartholin glands producing further lubrication, and the tissues of the outer third of the vagina swelling [N5-F3]. The Cleveland Clinic also notes that the vaginal walls turn darker and that muscle tension continues to increase [N1-F1]. The evidence explicitly frames the plateau as the period of sexual excitement prior to orgasm [N5-F3].

**Orgasm phase**: Orgasm is marked by involuntary muscle contractions and a sudden release of tension. In men, orgasm is usually associated with ejaculation, with the evidence describing the ejaculation of semen from the penis [N5-F3]. In women, orgasm is described as the culmination of sexual arousal, and the evidence notes that the vaginal muscles contract and that the body may experience a rash or “sex flush” [N1-F1][N5-F3]. The evidence also notes that some females can return to the orgasm phase with further stimulation and may experience additional orgasms, while males typically enter a refractory period after orgasm [N1-F1].

**Resolution phase**: After orgasm, the body returns to its normal state. The evidence notes that swollen or erect genital parts return to their previous size or position, and people may feel satisfaction or fatigue [N1-F1]. The Cleveland Clinic also emphasizes that the order and timing of the stages can vary and that some stages may be absent or out of sequence in certain encounters [N1-F1].

### How arousal spreads from the brain to the genital tract

The evidence indicates that arousal spreads through a coordinated pathway from the brain to the genital tract. In the excitement phase, the body prepares for sexual intercourse, and physical or mental erotic stimuli lead to sexual arousal [N5-F3]. The evidence also notes that the excitement phase is the result of physical or mental erotic stimuli such as kissing, making out, fantasizing, or viewing erotic images [N5-F3]. This implies that the brain processes erotic input, which then activates autonomic and genital responses. The Cleveland Clinic describes the arousal phase as “the first stage of the human sexual response cycle” that occurs as a result of such stimuli [N1-R1][N5-F3].

The anatomical evidence further supports a brain-to-genital pathway by describing how arousal is accompanied by increased heart rate, breathing, and vasocongestion, as well as muscle tension and the sex flush [N2-F2][N5-F3]. The evidence also notes that the excitement phase is followed by the plateau phase, where sensations heighten before climax [N2-R5]. This sequence suggests a progression from central stimulation to genital engorgement and heightened sensitivity.

### Differences between male and female anatomical involvement

The evidence clearly distinguishes male and female anatomical involvement. In men, arousal involves penile erection, cremaster reflex, and pre-ejaculate [N2-R2][N2-R4]. In women, it involves clitoral tumescence, genital vasocongestion, increased vaginal lubrication, and breast changes [N2-R2][N2-R4]. The Cleveland Clinic explicitly notes that these changes can vary in timing and intensity, and that men and women can experience the same phases even if the timing differs [N1-F1].

The evidence also highlights sex differences in the likelihood of orgasm during intercourse. In men, orgasm is more reliably achieved through sexual intercourse, while in women, orgasm during intercourse is highly variable and influenced by factors such as clitoral stimulation and genital anatomy [N2-F2]. This distinction is important because it shows that the anatomical structures involved in orgasm are not identical between the sexes and that the pathways to orgasm may differ.

In summary, the anatomical sequence is: brain/central stimulation → erection/vasocongestion → genital engorgement and sensitivity → orgasmic contractions → resolution [N2-R2][N2-R4][N5-F3]. The evidence also underscores that the sequence is not universal and that the exact timing and intensity vary across individuals and sexes [N1-F1][N2-F2].

## Sequential physiology of human sexual response

The physiological characterization of the human sexual response sequence is supported by both the general sexual-response-cycle evidence and the neurophysiology/hormone evidence. The cycle is described as a sequence of physical and emotional changes from the sexually unaroused to aroused state and resolution [N1-R2]. The neurophysiology evidence adds that sexual arousal depends on neural, hormonal, genetic, and environmental factors, with the human case involving complex influences [N3-R1]. The hormone and neurotransmitter evidence further emphasizes that sexual activity is mediated by hormones and neurotransmitters, which increase arousal and sexual behavior [N3-R4].

### Neurochemical and hormonal changes across phases

The evidence suggests that the sequence is shaped by a combination of hormones and neurotransmitters, though the exact substances vary by phase. The neurophysiology source states that sexual arousal is dependent on neural (sensory and cognitive) factors, hormonal factors, genetic factors, and environmental influences [N3-R1]. The hormone/transmitter source notes that sexual activity is sublimated through the effects of hormones and neurotransmitters, which increase arousal [N3-R4]. While the evidence does not provide a phase-specific hormone list in the provided excerpts, it clearly frames arousal as a hormonally and neurochemically mediated process.

The brain regions and autonomic nervous system evidence is more specific. The brainfacts.org source notes that brain regions such as the hypothalamus, amygdala, and hippocampus contain estrogen and progesterone receptors [N3-R2]. This is relevant because these brain structures are likely involved in regulating sexual desire, motivation, and arousal. The neuroanatomy source notes brain activation and sexual arousal in healthy, heterosexual males under different hormonal conditions [N3-R3], indicating that the brain is central to the physiological sequence.

The autonomic nervous system is also central. The neurophysiology of male sexual arousal source defines sexual arousal as an overall autonomic nervous system response leading to penile erection, triggered selectively by specific sexual cues [N3-R5]. This is consistent with the general cycle evidence, which describes increased heart rate, breathing, and blood pressure as arousal progresses [N2-F2][N5-F3]. The evidence therefore supports a model in which the sympathetic nervous system drives arousal, while parasympathetic and autonomic pathways regulate erection and other genital responses.

### How arousal, plateau, orgasm, and resolution differ physiologically

The evidence describes each phase as physiologically distinct, even if they overlap in some ways.

- **Arousal**: This phase is marked by increased heart rate, breathing, blood pressure, and genital vasocongestion [N2-F2][N5-F3]. In men, penile erection and pre-ejaculate appear early [N2-R2][N2-R4]. In women, clitoral tumescence, vaginal lubrication, and breast changes occur [N2-R2][N2-R4]. The evidence also notes that the excitement phase is the first stage of the cycle and that the body prepares for sexual intercourse [N5-F3].

- **Plateau**: This phase intensifies arousal and is described as the period of sexual excitement prior to orgasm [N5-F3]. The evidence notes that respiration, heart rate, and muscle tension continue to increase, and that prolonged time in the plateau phase may result in sexual frustration [N5-F3]. In men, the urethral sphincter contracts and rhythmic contractions begin at the base of the penis; in women, the clitoris becomes extremely sensitive and the Bartholin glands produce more lubrication [N5-F3].

- **Orgasm**: Orgasm is described as the climax of the cycle, with the shortest duration among the phases [N1-F1]. It is marked by involuntary muscle contractions, increased heart rate, and a sudden release of tension [N1-F1][N5-F3]. In men, orgasm is usually associated with ejaculation [N5-F3]. In women, orgasm is the culmination of sexual arousal, with vaginal muscle contractions and possible skin changes [N1-F1][N5-F3].

- **Resolution**: In this phase, the body returns to its normal state. The evidence notes that swollen or erect genital parts return to their previous size or position, and that people may feel satisfaction or fatigue [N1-F1]. The Cleveland Clinic also emphasizes that the sequence can vary and that some stages may be absent or out of sequence [N1-F1].

### Role of autonomic nervous system and brain regions

The autonomic nervous system is central to the sequence. The male sexual-arousal source defines sexual arousal as an overall autonomic nervous system response leading to penile erection [N3-R5]. This aligns with the broader cycle evidence, which describes vasocongestion, increased heart rate, and increased breathing as arousal progresses [N2-F2][N5-F3]. The brain regions evidence is also important: the hypothalamus, amygdala, and hippocampus contain estrogen and progesterone receptors [N3-R2]. These regions are likely involved in processing sexual stimuli, regulating desire, and integrating hormonal signals.

The evidence therefore supports a physiology model in which the brain receives erotic input, processes it through limbic and hypothalamic structures, and then activates autonomic pathways that drive genital engorgement, erection, and orgasmic contractions. Hormones and neurotransmitters appear to modulate this sequence, while the autonomic nervous system executes the immediate physiological changes [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R5].

In short, the physiological sequence is: central stimulation → autonomic activation and genital vasocongestion → heightened arousal/plateau → orgasmic climax → autonomic return to baseline [N2-F2][N3-R2][N3-R5].

## Sequential psychology of human sexual response

The psychological evidence shows that sexual response is not purely physiological; cognition, emotion, and motivation are deeply embedded in each phase. The general cycle evidence notes that the sexual response cycle consists of desire, arousal, orgasm, and resolution, and that people experience the cycle differently [N1-R1][N1-R3]. The psychology-related evidence also emphasizes that sexual arousal is described as the physiological and psychological responses in preparation for sexual intercourse or when exposed to sexual stimuli [N4-R1]. It further notes that emotional intimacy is a key motivator of sexual activity, especially for women with arousal or desire disorders [N4-R3].

### How cognition, emotion, and motivation shape each phase

**Desire/arousal phase**: The evidence suggests that desire and arousal are closely linked to motivation and erotic stimuli. The general cycle source states that the cycle begins with desire or excitement, and that physical or mental erotic stimuli such as kissing, making out, fantasizing, or viewing erotic images lead to sexual arousal [N1-R1][N5-F3]. The evidence also notes that desire may be motivated by intimacy rather than pure physical arousal in some individuals [N1-F1]. This means that motivation and mental imagery can initiate or enhance the desire/arousal phase.

**Plateau phase**: The plateau phase is described as the period of sexual excitement prior to orgasm [N5-F3]. The psychology evidence indicates that sexual arousal and desire respond to different sexual stimuli, including erotic stories, unstructured fantasy, and imagined social situations [N4-R4]. This implies that the plateau is not only a physiological intensification but also a cognitive-emotional phase in which fantasy, memory, and imagined scenarios can shape the experience.

**Orgasm phase**: Orgasm is framed as the climax of the cycle, but the evidence also suggests that psychological factors can influence whether and how strongly it is experienced. The evidence notes that the promise of orgasm may provide primary motivation for individuals to engage in sexual intercourse [N2-F2], and that sexual arousal itself is rewarding [N2-F2]. This indicates that motivation, expectation, and reward mechanisms contribute to the orgasm phase.

**Resolution phase**: The evidence notes that people may feel satisfaction or fatigue after resolution [N1-F1]. This emotional aftermath is consistent with the idea that the sexual sequence is not only about climax but also about the psychological aftermath of the encounter. The evidence also emphasizes that the order and timing of the stages can vary, which means that psychological states such as fatigue, relaxation, or emotional dissatisfaction can affect how resolution is experienced [N1-F1].

### Role of intimacy, anxiety, and arousal regulation

Intimacy is explicitly identified as a key motivator of sexual activity, especially for women with arousal or desire disorders [N4-R3]. This suggests that the psychological sequence is shaped by the emotional context of the relationship. The evidence also notes that the sexual response cycle is not a one-size-fits-all model and that people experience it differently [N1-F1]. This supports the idea that intimacy, trust, and emotional connection can enhance the sequence, while anxiety or discomfort can disrupt it.

Anxiety is implied as a disruptive factor through the broader discussion of variability and individual differences. The cycle evidence notes that some people may skip a phase entirely, some may experience it during certain encounters only, and the order may be out of sequence [N1-F1]. This variability can reflect anxiety, performance pressure, or emotional regulation difficulties. The psychology evidence also suggests that arousal and desire respond to sexual stimuli in complex ways [N4-R4], which means that anxiety can interfere with the ability to regulate arousal or maintain a consistent sequence.

Arousal regulation is another psychological component. The evidence notes that the desire/arousal phase may come after arousal in some people, and that the intensity of the response varies [N1-F1]. This indicates that individuals can regulate their arousal through cognitive and emotional strategies, but the sequence is not always linear or predictable [N1-F1]. The evidence also notes that some people may not consistently experience changes during the desire phase [N1-F1], which suggests that regulation can be inconsistent across individuals.

### How psychological state can disrupt or enhance the sequence

The evidence clearly supports the idea that psychological state can disrupt the sequence. The general cycle source states that the order and timing can vary and that some stages may be absent or out of sequence [N1-F1]. The psychology evidence further notes that emotional intimacy is especially motivating for women with arousal and desire disorders [N4-R3], implying that a lack of intimacy or emotional connection can weaken the sequence. Conversely, the evidence also shows that sexual arousal can be rewarding and that desire is shaped by multiple stimuli [N2-F2][N4-R4], which can enhance the sequence.

In summary, the psychological sequence is: motivation/intimacy → cognitive/emotional arousal → fantasy/imagination during plateau → reward/excitement during orgasm → emotional satisfaction or fatigue during resolution [N1-R1][N4-R1][N4-R3][N4-R4]. The evidence also indicates that anxiety, emotional regulation, and individual differences can make the sequence less linear, more variable, or even absent in some encounters [N1-F1][N4-R3].

## Model-based sequence and controversies

The model-based evidence shows that the sexual-response-cycle sequence is historically and currently debated. The general cycle evidence notes that the four-phase model is not a one-size-fits-all model and that people experience it differently [N1-F1]. The Wikipedia source states that the human sexual response cycle is a four-stage model of physiological responses to sexual stimulation, first formulated by Masters and Johnson in 1966 [N5-R2][N5-F3]. However, other models have been formulated by scholars who have criticized inaccuracies in the Masters-Johnson model [N5-R3].

### How Masters-Johnson and other models sequence the phases

Masters and Johnson’s model is the most widely referenced in the evidence. The source explicitly states that they identified four successive stages: excitement, plateau, orgasm, and resolution [N5-R5]. The Wikipedia source describes the same four-phase sequence: excitement, plateau, orgasmic, and resolution [N5-R2][N5-F3]. The evidence also notes that Masters and Johnson’s model was first formulated in their 1966 book Human Sexual Response [N5-F3].

Other models are described as alternatives or refinements. The evidence notes that the remaining two phases of Kaplan’s triphasic model essentially represented an amalgamation of the excitement, plateau, orgasm, and resolution phases [N5-R3]. This indicates that some later models collapsed or reorganized the four-phase sequence rather than replacing it. The evidence also notes that the cycle is described as a four-stage model of physiological responses to sexual stimulation, and that other scholars have criticized certain inaccuracies in the model [N5-R2][N5-R3].

### Where the sequence is disputed or oversimplified

The evidence repeatedly emphasizes that the sequence is disputed and oversimplified. The general cycle source states that the sequence is not a one-size-fits-all model and that people experience the cycle differently [N1-F1]. The Wikipedia source explicitly states that the model was first formulated by Masters and Johnson, and that other scholars have criticized certain inaccuracies in it [N5-R2][N5-R3]. The evidence also notes that the order and timing can vary, and that some stages may be absent or out of sequence in certain encounters [N1-F1].

These criticisms suggest that the four-phase model may oversimplify the complexity of sexual response. The evidence also indicates that sexual arousal and desire can respond to different types of stimuli, including erotic stories, fantasy, and imagined social situations [N4-R4], which implies that the sequence is not always linear or uniform. The evidence further notes that the cycle may not be the most useful framework for all individuals because it is not universal [N1-F1].

### How the model relates to gender differences and non-binary experiences

The evidence shows that the model is not neutral with respect to sex and gender. The general cycle source notes that the four phases are experienced differently by men and women, and that the timing may differ [N1-F1]. The anatomy evidence also highlights that men and women have different anatomical involvement, with men experiencing penile erection, cremaster reflex, and pre-ejaculate, while women experience clitoral tumescence, genital vasocongestion, and increased vaginal lubrication [N2-R2][N2-R4]. The evidence also notes that orgasm during intercourse is highly variable in women and that some women may never experience orgasm in intercourse [N2-F2]. This indicates that the model can obscure sex differences rather than clarify them.

The evidence also implies that non-binary experiences are not explicitly addressed in the four-phase model. The evidence states that the sequence is not a one-size-fits-all model and that people experience it differently [N1-F1]. This suggests that the model may not fully capture the diversity of non-binary sexual experiences, including different anatomical pathways, arousal patterns, and sexual responses. The evidence does not provide a direct source on non-binary anatomy, but it does support the broader point that the sequence can vary across individuals and that the model should be interpreted cautiously [N1-F1][N5-F3].

In conclusion, the model-based sequence is: excitement → plateau → orgasm → resolution, with Masters-Johnson as the canonical source [N5-R2][N5-F3]. The evidence, however, indicates that the sequence is disputed, oversimplified, and sex-dependent [N1-F1][N5-R3][N2-F2]. It also suggests that the model may not fully accommodate non-binary experiences because the evidence focuses primarily on male and female anatomy and variability [N1-F1][N2-R2][N2-R4].

## Individual and sex differences in the sequence

The evidence shows that the sexual response sequence varies across men, women, and non-binary people, and that the sequence is not always linear or consistent. The general cycle evidence explicitly states that the order and timing can vary, that some stages may be absent, and that the sequence may be out of sequence in certain encounters [N1-F1]. The evidence also notes that the sequence is not a one-size-fits-all model [N1-F1].

### How the sequence varies across men, women, and non-binary people

**Men**: In men, the sequence is marked by penile erection, cremaster reflex, pre-ejaculate, and ejaculation during orgasm [N2-R2][N2-R4]. The evidence also notes that males typically need recovery time after orgasm, called a refractory period, and that this varies with age [N1-F1]. The evidence further suggests that men’s sexual response is more reliably tied to intercourse than women’s [N2-F2].

**Women**: In women, the sequence is described as beginning with clitoral tumescence, genital vasocongestion, increased vaginal lubrication, and breast changes [N2-R2][N2-R4]. The evidence also notes that orgasm during intercourse is highly variable in women and that some women may never experience orgasm in intercourse [N2-F2]. This indicates that the sequence can be less consistent in women compared to men.

**Non-binary people**: The evidence does not provide a direct source on non-binary anatomy or physiology, but it does support the broader conclusion that the sequence is not universal and that people experience it differently [N1-F1]. The evidence also states that the sexual response cycle is not a one-size-fits-all model [N1-F1]. This implies that non-binary experiences may differ from the standard male/female sequence and may involve different anatomical pathways, arousal patterns, and responses.

### When the sequence is not linear or consistent

The evidence is explicit that the sequence can be nonlinear and inconsistent. The general cycle source notes that some people may skip a phase entirely, some may experience it during certain encounters only, and that the order may be out of sequence [N1-F1]. The evidence also states that the order and timing can vary [N1-F1]. This variability suggests that the sequence is not always a clean progression from desire to orgasm to resolution, and that individuals may move between phases or experience them in different orders.

The evidence further notes that some people may not consistently experience changes during the desire phase [N1-F1]. This indicates that the sequence can be inconsistent even before reaching orgasm. The plateau phase is also described as a period of sexual excitement prior to orgasm, and the evidence notes that prolonged time in the plateau phase may result in sexual frustration [N5-F3]. This shows that the sequence can be disrupted by psychological or physiological factors.

### How cultural and individual factors affect interpretation

# How the human sexual response is sequentially characterized in anatomy, physiology, and psychology

The human sexual response is conventionally described as a sequence of phases that progress from desire or arousal through climax and resolution. Across the branch reports, the evidence consistently supports a four-phase model: **desire/arousal**, **plateau**, **orgasm**, and **resolution** [N1-R1][N1-R3][N1-F1]. However, the reports also emphasize that this sequence is not universal and can vary widely in timing, intensity, and order [N1-F1]. The integrated answer below synthesizes the anatomical, physiological, and psychological dimensions of each phase, and places the sequence in the context of models, controversies, and individual/sex differences.

---

## 1) Sequential anatomy: which structures are active in each phase

The anatomical evidence shows that the sexual response is a coordinated process involving both the brain and the genital tract [N2-R2][N2-R4][N5-F3]. In the first phase, the body prepares for sexual intercourse through central stimulation, and this activates genital structures.

### Desire/arousal phase
In men, this phase begins with **penile erection**, **cremaster reflex**, and **pre-ejaculate** [N2-R2][N2-R4]. In women, it involves **clitoral tumescence**, **genital vasocongestion**, **increased vaginal lubrication**, and breast changes such as **hardened nipples** and **fuller breasts** [N2-R2][N2-R4]. The Cleveland Clinic also notes that the clitoris swells and the vagina swells with increased blood flow, while the breasts become fuller in women [N1-F1]. In men, the testicles may swell or the scrotum may tighten, and the penis may begin to secrete lubricating fluid [N1-F1].

### Plateau phase
The plateau intensifies arousal. In men, the **urethral sphincter contracts**, and muscles at the base of the penis begin rhythmic contractions; the testicles rise closer to the body [N5-F3]. In women, the plateau continues the excitement-phase changes, with the clitoris becoming extremely sensitive, the Bartholin glands producing further lubrication, and the tissues of the outer third of the vagina swelling [N5-F3]. The evidence also notes that the vaginal walls turn darker and that muscle tension continues to increase [N1-F1].

### Orgasm phase
Orgasm is marked by involuntary muscle contractions and a sudden release of tension. In men, orgasm is usually associated with **ejaculation**, with the evidence describing the ejaculation of semen from the penis [N5-F3]. In women, orgasm is the culmination of sexual arousal, with **vaginal muscle contractions** and possible skin changes such as a rash or “sex flush” [N1-F1][N5-F3]. The evidence also notes that some females can return to the orgasm phase with further stimulation and may experience additional orgasms, while males typically enter a refractory period after orgasm [N1-F1].

### Resolution phase
After orgasm, the body returns to its normal state. The evidence notes that swollen or erect genital parts return to their previous size or position, and people may feel satisfaction or fatigue [N1-F1]. The Cleveland Clinic also emphasizes that the order and timing of the stages can vary and that some stages may be absent or out of sequence in certain encounters [N1-F1].

### How arousal spreads from the brain to the genital tract
The evidence indicates that arousal spreads through a coordinated pathway from the brain to the genital tract. The excitement phase is described as resulting from **physical or mental erotic stimuli** such as kissing, making out, fantasizing, or viewing erotic images [N5-F3]. This implies that the brain processes erotic input, which then activates autonomic and genital responses. The evidence also notes that the excitement phase is the first stage of the cycle and that the body prepares for sexual intercourse [N5-F3].

The anatomical evidence further supports a brain-to-genital pathway by describing increased heart rate, breathing, and vasocongestion, as well as muscle tension and the sex flush [N2-F2][N5-F3]. The evidence also notes that the excitement phase is followed by the plateau phase, where sensations heighten before climax [N2-R5]. This sequence suggests a progression from central stimulation to genital engorgement and heightened sensitivity.

### Differences between male and female anatomical involvement
The evidence clearly distinguishes male and female anatomical involvement. In men, arousal involves penile erection, cremaster reflex, and pre-ejaculate [N2-R2][N2-R4]. In women, it involves clitoral tumescence, genital vasocongestion, increased vaginal lubrication, and breast changes [N2-R2][N2-R4]. The Cleveland Clinic explicitly notes that these changes can vary in timing and intensity, and that men and women can experience the same phases even if the timing differs [N1-F1].

The evidence also highlights sex differences in the likelihood of orgasm during intercourse. In men, orgasm is more reliably achieved through sexual intercourse, while in women, orgasm during intercourse is highly variable and influenced by factors such as clitoral stimulation and genital anatomy [N2-F2]. This distinction is important because it shows that the anatomical structures involved in orgasm are not identical between the sexes and that the pathways to orgasm may differ.

## 2) Sequential physiology: neurochemical, hormonal, and autonomic changes

The physiological evidence frames the sexual response as a sequence of changing states that depend on **neural, hormonal, genetic, and environmental** factors [N3-R1]. It also emphasizes that sexual activity is mediated by **hormones and neurotransmitters**, which increase arousal and sexual behavior [N3-R4]. The brain regions evidence adds that structures such as the **hypothalamus, amygdala, and hippocampus** contain **estrogen and progesterone receptors** [N3-R2], which are relevant to sexual motivation and arousal. The neuroanatomy evidence also notes brain activation and sexual arousal in healthy, heterosexual males under different hormonal conditions [N3-R3].

The autonomic nervous system is central to the sequence. The male sexual-arousal source defines sexual arousal as an **overall autonomic nervous system response** leading to penile erection, triggered selectively by specific sexual cues [N3-R5]. This is consistent with the broader cycle evidence, which describes increased heart rate, breathing, and blood pressure as arousal progresses [N2-F2][N5-F3]. The evidence therefore supports a model in which the **sympathetic nervous system** drives arousal, while parasympathetic and autonomic pathways regulate erection and other genital responses.

### How the phases differ physiologically
The evidence describes each phase as physiologically distinct.

- **Arousal**: This phase is marked by increased heart rate, breathing, blood pressure, and genital vasocongestion [N2-F2][N5-F3]. In men, penile erection and pre-ejaculate appear early [N2-R2][N2-R4]. In women, clitoral tumescence, vaginal lubrication, and breast changes occur [N2-R2][N2-R4].
- **Plateau**: This phase intensifies arousal and is described as the period of sexual excitement prior to orgasm [N5-F3]. The evidence notes that respiration, heart rate, and muscle tension continue to increase, and prolonged time in the plateau phase may result in sexual frustration [N5-F3]. In men, the urethral sphincter contracts and rhythmic contractions begin at the base of the penis; in women, the clitoris becomes extremely sensitive and the Bartholin glands produce more lubrication [N5-F3].
- **Orgasm**: Orgasm is described as the climax of the cycle, with the shortest duration among the phases [N1-F1]. It is marked by involuntary muscle contractions, increased heart rate, and a sudden release of tension [N1-F1][N5-F3]. In men, orgasm is usually associated with ejaculation [N5-F3]. In women, orgasm is the culmination of sexual arousal, with vaginal muscle contractions and possible skin changes [N1-F1][N5-F3].
- **Resolution**: In this phase, the body returns to its normal state. The evidence notes that swollen or erect genital parts return to their previous size or position, and that people may feel satisfaction or fatigue [N1-F1]. The Cleveland Clinic also emphasizes that the sequence can vary and that some stages may be absent or out of sequence [N1-F1].

### Role of autonomic nervous system and brain regions
The autonomic nervous system is central to the sequence. The male sexual-arousal source defines sexual arousal as an overall autonomic nervous system response leading to penile erection [N3-R5]. This aligns with the broader cycle evidence, which describes vasocongestion, increased heart rate, and increased breathing as arousal progresses [N2-F2][N5-F3]. The brain regions evidence is also important: the hypothalamus, amygdala, and hippocampus contain estrogen and progesterone receptors [N3-R2]. These regions are likely involved in processing sexual stimuli, regulating desire, and integrating hormonal signals.

The evidence therefore supports a physiological model in which the brain receives erotic input, processes it through limbic and hypothalamic structures, and then activates autonomic pathways that drive genital engorgement, erection, and orgasmic contractions. Hormones and neurotransmitters appear to modulate this sequence, while the autonomic nervous system executes the immediate physiological changes [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R5].

## 3) Sequential psychology: cognition, emotion, and motivation

The psychological evidence shows that sexual response is not purely physiological; **cognition, emotion, and motivation** are deeply embedded in each phase [N4-R1][N4-R3]. The general cycle evidence notes that the sexual response cycle consists of desire, arousal, orgasm, and resolution, and that people experience the cycle differently [N1-R1][N1-R3]. The psychology-related evidence also emphasizes that sexual arousal is described as the **physiological and psychological responses** in preparation for sexual intercourse or when exposed to sexual stimuli [N4-R1].

### How cognition, emotion, and motivation shape each phase
**Desire/arousal phase**: The evidence suggests that desire and arousal are closely linked to motivation and erotic stimuli. The general cycle source states that the cycle begins with desire or excitement, and that physical or mental erotic stimuli such as kissing, making out, fantasizing, or viewing erotic images lead to sexual arousal [N1-R1][N5-F3]. The evidence also notes that desire may be motivated by intimacy rather than pure physical arousal in some individuals [N1-F1]. This means that motivation and mental imagery can initiate or enhance the desire/arousal phase.

**Plateau phase**: The plateau phase is described as the period of sexual excitement prior to orgasm [N5-F3]. The psychology evidence indicates that sexual arousal and desire respond to different sexual stimuli, including erotic stories, unstructured fantasy, and imagined social situations [N4-R4]. This implies that the plateau is not only a physiological intensification but also a cognitive-emotional phase in which fantasy, memory, and imagined scenarios can shape the experience.

**Orgasm phase**: Orgasm is framed as the climax of the cycle, but the evidence also suggests that psychological factors can influence whether and how strongly it is experienced. The evidence notes that the promise of orgasm may provide primary motivation for individuals to engage in sexual intercourse [N2-F2], and that sexual arousal itself is rewarding [N2-F2]. This indicates that motivation, expectation, and reward mechanisms contribute to the orgasm phase.

**Resolution phase**: The evidence notes that people may feel satisfaction or fatigue after resolution [N1-F1]. This emotional aftermath is consistent with the idea that the sexual sequence is not only about climax but also about the psychological aftermath of the encounter. The evidence also emphasizes that the order and timing of the stages can vary, which means that psychological states such as fatigue, relaxation, or emotional dissatisfaction can affect how resolution is experienced [N1-F1].

### Role of intimacy, anxiety, and arousal regulation
Intimacy is explicitly identified as a key motivator of sexual activity, especially for women with arousal or desire disorders [N4-R3]. This suggests that the psychological sequence is shaped by the emotional context of the relationship. The evidence also notes that the sexual response cycle is not a one-size-fits-all model and that people experience it differently [N1-F1]. This supports the idea that intimacy, trust, and emotional connection can enhance the sequence, while anxiety or discomfort can disrupt it.

Anxiety is implied as a disruptive factor through the broader discussion of variability and individual differences. The cycle evidence notes that some people may skip a phase entirely, some may experience it during certain encounters only, and the order may be out of sequence [N1-F1]. This variability can reflect anxiety, performance pressure, or emotional regulation difficulties. The psychology evidence also suggests that arousal and desire respond to sexual stimuli in complex ways [N4-R4], which means that anxiety can interfere with the ability to regulate arousal or maintain a consistent sequence.

The evidence clearly supports the idea that psychological state can disrupt the sequence. The general cycle source states that the order and timing can vary and that some stages may be absent or out of sequence [N1-F1]. The psychology evidence further notes that emotional intimacy is especially motivating for women with arousal and desire disorders [N4-R3], implying that a lack of intimacy or emotional connection can weaken the sequence. Conversely, the evidence also shows that sexual arousal can be rewarding and that desire is shaped by multiple stimuli [N2-F2][N4-R4], which can enhance the sequence.

## 4) Model-based sequence and controversies

The model-based evidence shows that the sexual-response-cycle sequence is historically and currently debated. The general cycle evidence notes that the four-phase model is not a one-size-fits-all model and that people experience it differently [N1-F1]. The Wikipedia source states that the human sexual response cycle is a four-stage model of physiological responses to sexual stimulation, first formulated by Masters and Johnson in 1966 [N5-R2][N5-F3]. However, other models have been formulated by scholars who have criticized inaccuracies in the Masters-Johnson model [N5-R3].

### How Masters-Johnson and other models sequence the phases
Masters and Johnson’s model is the most widely referenced in the evidence. The source explicitly states that they identified four successive stages: **excitement, plateau, orgasm, and resolution** [N5-R5]. The Wikipedia source describes the same four-phase sequence: **excitement, plateau, orgasmic, and resolution** [N5-R2][N5-F3]. The evidence also notes that Masters and Johnson’s model was first formulated in their 1966 book *Human Sexual Response* [N5-F3].

Other models are described as alternatives or refinements. The evidence notes that the remaining two phases of Kaplan’s triphasic model essentially represented an amalgamation of the excitement, plateau, orgasm, and resolution phases [N5-R3]. This indicates that some later models collapsed or reorganized the four-phase sequence rather than replacing it. The evidence also notes that the cycle is described as a four-stage model of physiological responses to sexual stimulation, and that other scholars have criticized certain inaccuracies in the model [N5-R2][N5-R3].

### Where the sequence is disputed or oversimplified
The evidence repeatedly emphasizes that the sequence is disputed and oversimplified. The general cycle source states that the sequence is not a one-size-fits-all model and that people experience it differently [N1-F1]. The Wikipedia source explicitly states that the model was first formulated by Masters and Johnson, and that other scholars have criticized certain inaccuracies in it [N5-R2][N5-R3]. The evidence also notes that the order and timing can vary, and that some stages may be absent or out of sequence in certain encounters [N1-F1].

### How the model relates to gender differences and non-binary experiences
The evidence shows that the model is not neutral with respect to sex and gender. The general cycle source notes that the four phases are experienced differently by men and women, and that the timing may differ [N1-F1]. The evidence also implies that non-binary experiences are not explicitly addressed in the four-phase model. ### How the sequence varies across men, women, and non-binary people
**Men**: In men, the sequence is marked by penile erection, cremaster reflex, pre-ejaculate, and ejaculation during orgasm [N2-R2][N2-R4]. The evidence also notes that males typically need recovery time after orgasm, called a refractory period, and that this varies with age [N1-F1]. **Non-binary people**: The evidence does not provide a direct source on non-binary anatomy or physiology, but it does support the broader conclusion that the sequence is not universal and that people experience it differently [N1-F1]. The evidence also states that the sexual response cycle is not a one-size-fits-all model [N1-F1]. ### How cultural and individual factors affect interpretation
Cultural and individual factors are central to how the sequence is interpreted. ## 6) Integrated conclusion

Taken together, the evidence supports a sequential characterization of the human sexual response that is anatomical, physiological, and psychological.

- **Anatomically**, the sequence involves distinct genital structures: penile erection and pre-ejaculate in men, clitoral tumescence and genital vasocongestion in women, and variable sensitivity and lubrication in both sexes [N2-R2][N2-R4][N5-F3].

- **In terms of differences**, the sequence varies across men, women, and non-binary people, and is often not linear or consistent; cultural and individual factors further affect interpretation [N1-F1][N5-F3].

## Sequential anatomy of human sexual response

The human sexual response sequence, as described in the evidence, is framed around four phases: desire/arousal, plateau, orgasm, and resolution, with the Cleveland Clinic and Wikipedia both identifying this as the standard model [N1-R1][N1-R3]. The anatomical evidence emphasizes that the response is not a single isolated event but a coordinated process involving the brain, genital tract, and autonomic nervous system [N2-R2][N2-R5].

### Anatomical structures active in each phase

**Desire/arousal phase**: The evidence shows that both men and women experience early physiological signs of arousal, including increased heart rate, breathing, and blood pressure [N2-F2][N5-F3]. In men, the phase begins with penile erection, cremaster reflex, and pre-ejaculate; in women, it involves clitoral tumescence, genital vasocongestion, increased vaginal lubrication, and breast changes such as hardened nipples and fuller breasts [N2-R2][N2-R4]. The Cleveland Clinic also notes that the clitoris swells and the vagina swells with increased blood flow, while the breasts become fuller in women [N1-F1]. For men, the testicles may swell or the scrotum may tighten, and the penis may begin to secrete lubricating fluid [N1-F1].

**Plateau phase**: This phase intensifies the arousal process. In men, the evidence states that the urethral sphincter contracts and muscles at the base of the penis begin rhythmic contractions, while the testicles rise closer to the body [N5-F3]. In women, the plateau stage continues the excitement phase changes, with the clitoris becoming extremely sensitive, the Bartholin glands producing further lubrication, and the tissues of the outer third of the vagina swelling [N5-F3]. The Cleveland Clinic also notes that the vaginal walls turn darker and that muscle tension continues to increase [N1-F1]. The evidence explicitly frames the plateau as the period of sexual excitement prior to orgasm [N5-F3].

**Orgasm phase**: Orgasm is marked by involuntary muscle contractions and a sudden release of tension. In men, orgasm is usually associated with ejaculation, with the evidence describing the ejaculation of semen from the penis [N5-F3]. In women, orgasm is described as the culmination of sexual arousal, and the evidence notes that the vaginal muscles contract and that the body may experience a rash or “sex flush” [N1-F1][N5-F3]. The evidence also notes that some females can return to the orgasm phase with further stimulation and may experience additional orgasms, while males typically enter a refractory period after orgasm [N1-F1].

**Resolution phase**: After orgasm, the body returns to its normal state. The evidence notes that swollen or erect genital parts return to their previous size or position, and people may feel satisfaction or fatigue [N1-F1]. The Cleveland Clinic also emphasizes that the order and timing of the stages can vary and that some stages may be absent or out of sequence in certain encounters [N1-F1].

### How arousal spreads from the brain to the genital tract

The evidence indicates that arousal spreads through a coordinated pathway from the brain to the genital tract. In the excitement phase, the body prepares for sexual intercourse, and physical or mental erotic stimuli lead to sexual arousal [N5-F3]. The evidence also notes that the excitement phase is the result of physical or mental erotic stimuli such as kissing, making out, fantasizing, or viewing erotic images [N5-F3]. This implies that the brain processes erotic input, which then activates autonomic and genital responses. The Cleveland Clinic describes the arousal phase as “the first stage of the human sexual response cycle” that occurs as a result of such stimuli [N1-R1][N5-F3].

The anatomical evidence further supports a brain-to-genital pathway by describing how arousal is accompanied by increased heart rate, breathing, and vasocongestion, as well as muscle tension and the sex flush [N2-F2][N5-F3]. The evidence also notes that the excitement phase is followed by the plateau phase, where sensations heighten before climax [N2-R5]. This sequence suggests a progression from central stimulation to genital engorgement and heightened sensitivity.

### Differences between male and female anatomical involvement

The evidence clearly distinguishes male and female anatomical involvement. In men, arousal involves penile erection, cremaster reflex, and pre-ejaculate [N2-R2][N2-R4]. In women, it involves clitoral tumescence, genital vasocongestion, increased vaginal lubrication, and breast changes [N2-R2][N2-R4]. The Cleveland Clinic explicitly notes that these changes can vary in timing and intensity, and that men and women can experience the same phases even if the timing differs [N1-F1].

The evidence also highlights sex differences in the likelihood of orgasm during intercourse. In men, orgasm is more reliably achieved through sexual intercourse, while in women, orgasm during intercourse is highly variable and influenced by factors such as clitoral stimulation and genital anatomy [N2-F2]. This distinction is important because it shows that the anatomical structures involved in orgasm are not identical between the sexes and that the pathways to orgasm may differ.

In summary, the anatomical sequence is: brain/central stimulation → erection/vasocongestion → genital engorgement and sensitivity → orgasmic contractions → resolution [N2-R2][N2-R4][N5-F3]. The evidence also underscores that the sequence is not universal and that the exact timing and intensity vary across individuals and sexes [N1-F1][N2-F2].

## Sequential physiology of human sexual response

The physiological characterization of the human sexual response sequence is supported by both the general sexual-response-cycle evidence and the neurophysiology/hormone evidence. The cycle is described as a sequence of physical and emotional changes from the sexually unaroused to aroused state and resolution [N1-R2]. The neurophysiology evidence adds that sexual arousal depends on neural, hormonal, genetic, and environmental factors, with the human case involving complex influences [N3-R1]. The hormone and neurotransmitter evidence further emphasizes that sexual activity is mediated by hormones and neurotransmitters, which increase arousal and sexual behavior [N3-R4].

### Neurochemical and hormonal changes across phases

The evidence suggests that the sequence is shaped by a combination of hormones and neurotransmitters, though the exact substances vary by phase. The neurophysiology source states that sexual arousal is dependent on neural (sensory and cognitive) factors, hormonal factors, genetic factors, and environmental influences [N3-R1]. The hormone/transmitter source notes that sexual activity is sublimated through the effects of hormones and neurotransmitters, which increase arousal [N3-R4]. While the evidence does not provide a phase-specific hormone list in the provided excerpts, it clearly frames arousal as a hormonally and neurochemically mediated process.

The brain regions and autonomic nervous system evidence is more specific. The brainfacts.org source notes that brain regions such as the hypothalamus, amygdala, and hippocampus contain estrogen and progesterone receptors [N3-R2]. This is relevant because these brain structures are likely involved in regulating sexual desire, motivation, and arousal. The neuroanatomy source notes brain activation and sexual arousal in healthy, heterosexual males under different hormonal conditions [N3-R3], indicating that the brain is central to the physiological sequence.

The autonomic nervous system is also central. The neurophysiology of male sexual arousal source defines sexual arousal as an overall autonomic nervous system response leading to penile erection, triggered selectively by specific sexual cues [N3-R5]. This is consistent with the general cycle evidence, which describes increased heart rate, breathing, and blood pressure as arousal progresses [N2-F2][N5-F3]. The evidence therefore supports a model in which the sympathetic nervous system drives arousal, while parasympathetic and autonomic pathways regulate erection and other genital responses.

### How arousal, plateau, orgasm, and resolution differ physiologically

The evidence describes each phase as physiologically distinct, even if they overlap in some ways.

- **Arousal**: This phase is marked by increased heart rate, breathing, blood pressure, and genital vasocongestion [N2-F2][N5-F3]. In men, penile erection and pre-ejaculate appear early [N2-R2][N2-R4]. In women, clitoral tumescence, vaginal lubrication, and breast changes occur [N2-R2][N2-R4]. The evidence also notes that the excitement phase is the first stage of the cycle and that the body prepares for sexual intercourse [N5-F3].

- **Plateau**: This phase intensifies arousal and is described as the period of sexual excitement prior to orgasm [N5-F3]. The evidence notes that respiration, heart rate, and muscle tension continue to increase, and that prolonged time in the plateau phase may result in sexual frustration [N5-F3]. In men, the urethral sphincter contracts and rhythmic contractions begin at the base of the penis; in women, the clitoris becomes extremely sensitive and the Bartholin glands produce more lubrication [N5-F3].

- **Orgasm**: Orgasm is described as the climax of the cycle, with the shortest duration among the phases [N1-F1]. It is marked by involuntary muscle contractions, increased heart rate, and a sudden release of tension [N1-F1][N5-F3]. In men, orgasm is usually associated with ejaculation [N5-F3]. In women, orgasm is the culmination of sexual arousal, with vaginal muscle contractions and possible skin changes [N1-F1][N5-F3].

- **Resolution**: In this phase, the body returns to its normal state. The evidence notes that swollen or erect genital parts return to their previous size or position, and that people may feel satisfaction or fatigue [N1-F1]. The Cleveland Clinic also emphasizes that the sequence can vary and that some stages may be absent or out of sequence [N1-F1].

### Role of autonomic nervous system and brain regions

The autonomic nervous system is central to the sequence. The male sexual-arousal source defines sexual arousal as an overall autonomic nervous system response leading to penile erection [N3-R5]. This aligns with the broader cycle evidence, which describes vasocongestion, increased heart rate, and increased breathing as arousal progresses [N2-F2][N5-F3]. The brain regions evidence is also important: the hypothalamus, amygdala, and hippocampus contain estrogen and progesterone receptors [N3-R2]. These regions are likely involved in processing sexual stimuli, regulating desire, and integrating hormonal signals.

The evidence therefore supports a physiology model in which the brain receives erotic input, processes it through limbic and hypothalamic structures, and then activates autonomic pathways that drive genital engorgement, erection, and orgasmic contractions. Hormones and neurotransmitters appear to modulate this sequence, while the autonomic nervous system executes the immediate physiological changes [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R5].

In short, the physiological sequence is: central stimulation → autonomic activation and genital vasocongestion → heightened arousal/plateau → orgasmic climax → autonomic return to baseline [N2-F2][N3-R2][N3-R5].

The general cycle source states that the cycle begins with desire or excitement, and that physical or mental erotic stimuli such as kissing, making out, fantasizing, or viewing erotic images lead to sexual arousal [N1-R1][N5-F3]. The evidence also notes that desire may be motivated by intimacy rather than pure physical arousal in some individuals [N1-F1]. This means that motivation and mental imagery can initiate or enhance the desire/arousal phase.

**Plateau phase**: The plateau phase is described as the period of sexual excitement prior to orgasm [N5-F3]. The psychology evidence indicates that sexual arousal and desire respond to different sexual stimuli, including erotic stories, unstructured fantasy, and imagined social situations [N4-R4]. This implies that the plateau is not only a physiological intensification but also a cognitive-emotional phase in which fantasy, memory, and imagined scenarios can shape the experience.

**Orgasm phase**: Orgasm is framed as the climax of the cycle, but the evidence also suggests that psychological factors can influence whether and how strongly it is experienced. The evidence notes that the promise of orgasm may provide primary motivation for individuals to engage in sexual intercourse [N2-F2], and that sexual arousal itself is rewarding [N2-F2]. This indicates that motivation, expectation, and reward mechanisms contribute to the orgasm phase.

**Resolution phase**: The evidence notes that people may feel satisfaction or fatigue after resolution [N1-F1]. This emotional aftermath is consistent with the idea that the sexual sequence is not only about climax but also about the psychological aftermath of the encounter. The evidence also emphasizes that the order and timing of the stages can vary, which means that psychological states such as fatigue, relaxation, or emotional dissatisfaction can affect how resolution is experienced [N1-F1].

Intimacy is explicitly identified as a key motivator of sexual activity, especially for women with arousal or desire disorders [N4-R3]. This suggests that the psychological sequence is shaped by the emotional context of the relationship. The psychology evidence also suggests that arousal and desire respond to sexual stimuli in complex ways [N4-R4], which means that anxiety can interfere with the ability to regulate arousal or maintain a consistent sequence.

Conversely, the evidence also shows that sexual arousal can be rewarding and that desire is shaped by multiple stimuli [N2-F2][N4-R4], which can enhance the sequence.

In summary, the psychological sequence is: motivation/intimacy → cognitive/emotional arousal → fantasy/imagination during plateau → reward/excitement during orgasm → emotional satisfaction or fatigue during resolution [N1-R1][N4-R1][N4-R3][N4-R4]. ### How Masters-Johnson and other models sequence the phases

Masters and Johnson’s model is the most widely referenced in the evidence. The source explicitly states that they identified four successive stages: excitement, plateau, orgasm, and resolution [N5-R5]. The Wikipedia source describes the same four-phase sequence: excitement, plateau, orgasmic, and resolution [N5-R2][N5-F3]. The evidence also notes that Masters and Johnson’s model was first formulated in their 1966 book Human Sexual Response [N5-F3].

Other models are described as alternatives or refinements. The evidence notes that the remaining two phases of Kaplan’s triphasic model essentially represented an amalgamation of the excitement, plateau, orgasm, and resolution phases [N5-R3]. This indicates that some later models collapsed or reorganized the four-phase sequence rather than replacing it. The evidence also notes that the cycle is described as a four-stage model of physiological responses to sexual stimulation, and that other scholars have criticized certain inaccuracies in the model [N5-R2][N5-R3].

### Where the sequence is disputed or oversimplified

The evidence repeatedly emphasizes that the sequence is disputed and oversimplified. The general cycle source states that the sequence is not a one-size-fits-all model and that people experience the cycle differently [N1-F1]. The Wikipedia source explicitly states that the model was first formulated by Masters and Johnson, and that other scholars have criticized certain inaccuracies in it [N5-R2][N5-R3]. The evidence also notes that the order and timing can vary, and that some stages may be absent or out of sequence in certain encounters [N1-F1].

These criticisms suggest that the four-phase model may oversimplify the complexity of sexual response. The evidence also indicates that sexual arousal and desire can respond to different types of stimuli, including erotic stories, fantasy, and imagined social situations [N4-R4], which implies that the sequence is not always linear or uniform. The evidence shows that the model is not neutral with respect to sex and gender. The evidence also notes that orgasm during intercourse is highly variable in women and that some women may never experience orgasm in intercourse [N2-F2]. The evidence states that the sequence is not a one-size-fits-all model and that people experience it differently [N1-F1]. The evidence does not provide a direct source on non-binary anatomy, but it does support the broader point that the sequence can vary across individuals and that the model should be interpreted cautiously [N1-F1][N5-F3].

In conclusion, the model-based sequence is: excitement → plateau → orgasm → resolution, with Masters-Johnson as the canonical source [N5-R2][N5-F3]. The evidence, however, indicates that the sequence is disputed, oversimplified, and sex-dependent [N1-F1][N5-R3][N2-F2].
